headline: Your AI Agent Passed Every Test but Still Failed in Production
summary: Traditional testing methods often fail to catch critical issues in probabilistic AI agents, leading to silent failures in production despite passing all tests. Learn about common failure patterns and how to mitigate them.
details: A sophisticated AI agent can pass all unit and integration tests, even in staging, only to fail, hallucinate, or degrade silently in production. This isn't a failure of testing discipline, but a failure of assumption.

Traditional test-based validation was built for deterministic systems, but modern AI agents are probabilistic, stateful, and deeply integrated with external APIs and evolving data. Applying the same mental model creates blind spots that only appear after deployment.

One common issue is context window truncation. Tests often use small, fixed prompts, while production involves hours of conversation history. An agent that passed with a short demo may misinterpret requests when history exceeds its effective context budget, leading to a gradual drift in relevance.

To mitigate context issues, instrument agents with `context_length` monitors and `truncation_point` logs. Implement synthetic stress tests that progressively increase history length to measure answer consistency and use sliding windows or summarization layers to manage active context.

Another pattern is stochasticity and reproducibility. LLMs are inherently probabilistic, but tests often lock temperature or use fixed seeds. In production, real temperature and user variance lead to inconsistent behavior across identical queries, which tests fail to catch.

Adopt a request-response fingerprinting system to hash full inputs and log model outputs, allowing exact replay of bugs in a deterministic environment. Add chaos testing that varies temperature and seed to map the probability distribution of critical paths.

Agents also fail due to tool interaction drift. Tests mock external tools, but in production, real APIs, databases, or search services return unexpected status codes, rate limits, or schema changes. The agent's plan can break mid-execution, leading to incomplete or stale answers.

Treat tool contracts as first-class tests using property-based testing for responses (valid range, schema, latency). Implement a tool-health dashboard to track success rates and schema drift, and wrap external calls in circuit-breakers for graceful degradation.
